Good morning! Is this seat free? I'm Frank, my wife and I are from Chicago, on the same tour as you.
Good morning, Frank. Please, sit down. I'm Rosangela, from Sao Paulo, and I'm here with my husband.
Is he coming down for breakfast? My wife, Susan, is still asleep, she's much slower in the morning than I am.
He's on the balcony with the sun. He doesn't speak English, so I do the talking for both of us. He's quieter than me, much quieter.
So you're the outgoing one. My younger brother is like you, he's more talkative than anybody in our family, and he gets along with everybody.
Then my son takes after me too. He speaks better English than I do, and he's very hardworking, but he's twenty-four, and he travels with his friends now.
And here you are in Italy without him. Good for you. Susan isn't as patient as I am with new languages, she just points at the menu and smiles.
My husband is the same. He's not as brave as me with English, but he's more easygoing than anybody I know, he's never in a hurry. Come and meet him after breakfast.

My name is Antonio, and for eighteen years I have carried coffee to the same breakfast room in Sorrento, so believe me when I tell you: I know people. Every morning I watch the tables, and I can tell you who is who before anybody says good morning. There is always one person who is more talkative than everybody else, who says good morning to the whole room, and there is always somebody quieter, behind the newspaper, who only wants the coffee. Neither one is better than the other. But here is the thing I have learned in eighteen years. The couples who enjoy the trip most are almost never the ones with the best English. They are the ones who talk about their people. A woman from Brazil sat at table nine last summer, with her husband. He did not speak one word of English, not one, and he was much shyer than she was. But she talked. She told me her husband was more easygoing than her, that he was never in a hurry, that he was happy on the balcony with the sun. She told me her son was more fluent than the whole family together, and that he was twenty-four now, and traveling with his friends. In ten minutes I knew her family better than I know some of my neighbors, and her English was still growing. So do not wait until your English is perfect to talk about the people you love. Tell me who your husband is. Tell me who is the patient one, and who is the stubborn one. That is not grammar. That is friendship, and it starts at breakfast.

I am Marina, I am seventy-one, and I travel with a husband who does not speak English. For a long time, that was the loneliest part of my trips. Somebody would smile at us in a hotel, or on a boat, and ask a friendly question, and I would answer with four words: I am Marina, from Brazil. And then the conversation would stop, because I had nothing else. I knew the words for the airport and the words for the hotel, but I had no words for the people I love, and so my husband would sit next to me like a piece of luggage, and the other people never met him. And then, on a bus in Portugal, a woman asked me about him. And instead of stopping at four words, I tried. I said: he is quieter than me, he is not as brave as me with languages, but he is more patient than anybody, and he is the most generous man I know. Three sentences. My English was not better that day than the day before, but everything changed. The woman laughed and said her husband was exactly the same, and we talked for an hour, and at the end she came to meet him. Here is what nobody tells you. To make a friend in another country, you do not need perfect grammar. You need to be able to say who your people are: who is the talkative one, who is shy, who is easygoing, who never changes his mind. Learn those five or six words, and you stop traveling as a tourist. You start traveling as a person with a family.
